output.headline: Ministers plan multibillion-pound package to help young people into work
output.bodyHtml:
Ministers are working up a multibillion-pound package of support to help young people into work, which would replace a key disability benefit for under-25s – already halved to £217 a month – under sweeping welfare changes, the Guardian has learned.

A government source said: ‘We will be bringing forward a comprehensive package of support and reform to tackle the scandal of a million young people not in education, employment or training. The details are yet to be decided, but we are committed to enabling work and opportunity, while always protecting those unable to work.’

A DWP spokesperson said: ‘The Milburn and Timms reviews, due in the autumn, will lay the foundation for sustainable reform, and we will not pre-empt their findings.

‘We are already changing the system through the youth guarantee, narrowing the gap between universal credit standard and health rates, restoring face-to-face assessments, and investing a record £3.5bn in employment support for disabled people and those with long-term conditions. We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work.’

The package’s extra support will include subsidised jobs for younger people, more targeted ‘back to work’ schemes and support with mental health, as part of a drive to help more of the nation’s one million 16 to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neets) back into the workplace.

Whitehall sources said the package of changes under debate was much bigger than previously thought, as Andy Burnham’s government hopes to persuade more people on benefits back into work.

The plans are still awaiting the conclusions of reviews by Alan Milburn, who is looking at young people’s employment, and the Timms panel, which is examining the personal independence payment (Pip), a non-means-tested benefit that helps sick and disabled people with support costs.

A central option under consideration for young people is offering intensive support to get into work in place of the health element of universal credit for claimants under 25, which has already been almost halved to £217 a month. The possibility of removing it for existing claimants – not just new ones – is also being looked at.

Ministers have spent weeks trying to persuade Labour MPs that the plans are about reform, and feel confident opposition has waned, even though the move could be fraught with political danger after last year’s dramatic welfare rebellion.

As part of the same package, officials are looking at a new system to replace the Pip, which is claimed by four million people, after attempts to change existing eligibility criteria were rejected by MPs last year.

Under one possible plan, those with the most severe and debilitating disabilities would not lose any money, while a separate regime would apply to the under-25 age group, with reduced or withdrawn entitlements for others.

Again, those with the most severe conditions would not lose money or be reassessed, as officials more broadly work up a new set of eligibility criteria and assessments for the extra costs of disability under the replacement system, looking at whether this would apply to all claimants of working age, or those below a cut-off point such as 50 or 60.

Officials have also been returning to the idea of cuts to the Motability scheme at a future budget, after axing tax breaks worth £300m. The scheme allows disabled people to use their Pip benefit to lease new cars for three years.

One Whitehall source said removing or further cutting the health element of universal credit for those older than 25 had been considered, but government sources said this was not on the table.

Officials have looked at systems in other countries, such as Denmark, which restricts access to its ‘disability pension’ for under-40s, who instead are given help with flexible jobs and training unless they have no ability permanently to work.

Ministers and officials are working on a bill encompassing the replacement for Pip and changes to the under-25 system, to be presented in the next session of parliament next year; the significant changes would need legislation.

Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, used his conference speech this week to describe changing the welfare system as a ‘moral crusade’, saying too many younger people were stuck claiming benefits for too long.

However, the scale of the plans could reignite concerns among Labour MPs about the impact on the cost of living for disabled people, particularly when Pip is a non-means-tested benefit that is unrelated to a person’s employment status.

Milburn has said that too few young people who moved on to disability benefits received help into work. Many became ‘trapped’ on benefits, with evidence showing half were not in work 15 years later, an outcome he called a ‘catastrophic failure’.

He appeared to hint at the potential political risks of cuts to benefits at a Labour party conference fringe meeting on youth employment on Monday, saying ‘when it comes to benefit cuts it will be tricky’ – but added that not acting would be financially unsustainable and worse for young people.

Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, has gone further by saying she would ban young people from signing straight on to the benefits system if her party won the next election, as part of a plan to cut £23bn from the welfare bill. Under-25s with less than six months of continuous employment would no longer be able to claim universal credit and would instead have to undergo intensive job coaching.

Reform UK plans to cut the overall welfare bill by £50bn, with Pip replaced by another cash benefit that would be restricted to only the ‘gravely ill and severely challenged’, while ‘lower level conditions’ would get support overseen by local authorities.

Polling suggests that while the public favours cutting the welfare bill overall, they believe that tackling the root causes of joblessness instead of cutting benefits is the best way to do it. Burnham has said he wanted to avoid ‘crude cuts’, and used his party conference speech to signal an overhaul of the welfare system to pay for an expansion of youth jobs and training support.

UK welfare spending has reached £333bn this year, with pensioners receiving roughly 55 per cent of the budget, and young people including Neets – but not children – about 2.5 per cent. Milburn said it was ‘shameful’ the government spent 25 times as much on benefits for them than it did on supporting them into work.

More than 40 of the UK’s leading charities warned ministers earlier this year against imposing tougher benefit sanctions or cuts on disabled young people.

In their joint letter to Milburn and McFadden, they said cutting support or bringing in sanctions risked pushing thousands of vulnerable youngsters deeper into poverty and further away from employment.

The disability charity Scope has estimated about half of households with an under-22 receiving the universal credit health element are already in poverty, which it said could rise to more than nine in 10 if support was removed.

Campaigners warned that any move to cut benefits or increase conditionality rules was likely to drive many youngsters further away from the jobs market.

Lucy Schonegevel, the director of impact at Action for Children, said: ‘We are deeply concerned by reports that disability benefits for under-25s could be cut. If confirmed, that would be at odds with the prime minister’s recent warning against “crude cuts” … Serious investment in high quality, tailored employment support is vital, but employment support alone cannot overcome a lack of jobs.’

About 184,000 young people in the UK aged 16-24 receive the universal credit health element. The government has already cut this benefit, having previously announced a 50 per cent reduction to £217 a month for most new claimants from next April.
output.standfirst: Exclusive: Ministers are drawing up a multibillion-pound jobs scheme as part of welfare changes that could scrap a key disability benefit for under-25s, already halved to £217 a month, which charities say could deepen poverty.
output.progress: The government is already running a youth guarantee and investing a record £3.5bn in employment support for disabled people.

context.text: Alan Milburn's youth employment review will recommend fast-track, unconditional benefit access for young people with the most severe and lifelong disabilities, avoiding repeated assessments.

output.headline: Detectives widen Fairford investigation, making new arrest in Westminster
output.bodyHtml:
Detectives have arrested a dual UK-Iranian national on suspicion of terrorism offences, as part of an investigation into a suspected plot near RAF Fairford.

Counter-terrorism police said the 25-year-old man was arrested on Thursday in Westminster on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts under section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006.

Announcing the most recent arrest, Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism police, said: ‘As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.’

Evans added: ‘The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of inquiry.’

Counter-terrorism police said two properties had been searched in Westminster, London.

Five men in their 20s were arrested in the village of Whelford, Gloucestershire, outside the RAF base in the early hours of Sunday after police were alerted to suspicious vans in the area. They were released on police bail.

Searches of the vans, and of addresses linked to the men across London, found no evidence of a viable device. That examination led to the decision on Monday to bail the men, who had first been arrested on explosives charges and then later for preparing acts of terrorism.

Counter-terrorism police are leading the investigation, which is trying to establish why the five men, all British nationals from London, were in the Gloucestershire countryside, close to a sensitive site in the middle of the night.

One of the five men arrested near the base had called the police himself to report the incident, it emerged on Tuesday.

A farmer driving home from a party at about 1am on Sunday spotted the men and vans and called 999, it was revealed on Sunday.

The vans were marked with the logo of a legitimate fuel transit company that later denied ownership of the vehicles.

Andy Burnham called a meeting of Cobra, the government’s crisis committee, on Monday, attended by senior police and security officials – a decision driven by the mounting view among investigators that Iran was likely involved.

The police and security services’ investigation continues, with an Iranian link to the events in the Gloucestershire countryside over the weekend considered increasingly likely. Senior US politicians, including the president, Donald Trump, have expressed surprise that the suspects were released on bail.

Tensions have been high at RAF Fairford since Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in July that the base was a legitimate target. Iran’s embassy in London has denied any involvement in the events of the past few days.

The Iranian embassy in London has said it ‘categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations’ of Iranian involvement.

Ministers have been briefed that Iran has various reasons for hiring proxies, who sometimes are unwitting, to carry out acts that aim to eat up resources and create chaos.

People detained for terrorism offences can be detained under two legal schedules that dictate how long they can be held without charge.

Under the terrorism schedule, a suspect can be held for up to 14 days but cannot be bailed.

The 25-year-old man arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts is being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (Pace), a spokesperson for CTP said.

That means he could be released on bail under investigation, but detectives have much less time to hold him.

The five men arrested early on Sunday in the Gloucestershire countryside were held under Pace before being bailed the next day.

The bomb squad and counter-terror police descended on Whelford on Sunday, and 85 households were forced to decamp to a leisure centre.

Some of the evacuated residents were able to stay with families, about 60 people received support from a Cotswold district council rest centre in Cirencester, and 28 people were accommodated overnight in hotels.
output.standfirst: Counter-terrorism police say they are pursuing every line of inquiry, including possible foreign state involvement, as they arrest a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national in Westminster and search two properties in central London.
output.progress: Counter-terrorism specialists are pursuing multiple lines of inquiry, including possible foreign state involvement, after arresting a new suspect in Westminster.

output.headline: France opens internal investigation into force used by officers against three pupils
output.bodyHtml:
The French government has said many schools will switch to online classes to protect teachers and pupils, as a fast-growing protest by high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities escalated into what it called “urban violence”, with nearly 3,000 students detained nationwide.

The interior ministry has announced an internal investigation into accusations of excessive force and brutality by officers against three pupils; injuries have mainly been from hurled objects, but some have come from police-fired riot-control projectiles.

The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, called a crisis cabinet meeting on Thursday and told ministers to cancel travel plans to deal with the demonstrations, which erupted in the Paris region last week but have snowballed across the country.

Lecornu’s office said: “This upsurge in violence makes it virtually impossible to maintain the continuity of public education and is exposing staff and students to danger.” The education minister, Édouard Geffray, is to meet pupil representatives on Friday.

About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents were under way outside high schools around the country, police said, with more than 160 shut down as a result. Access was also blocked to about 30 university campuses on Thursday, including in Paris and Marseille.

Nearly 3,000 lycée students – aged between 15 and 18 – have been detained since the start of the protests, including 1,949 on Thursday alone, the interior ministry said. More than 300 police and dozens of firefighters, teachers and pupils have been injured.

The pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves earlier this year. Riot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests.

Rubbish bins have been set on fire outside many schools and more serious arson attempts have been reported inside some buildings. Fire damage in one school in Nantes in the north-west was so extensive that it will stay closed for a month, authorities said.

In the northern city of Caen, 16-year-old Maelle said she wished those setting bins on fire would protest “with words”. Students were protesting “against this government that doesn’t invest in heating, air conditioning, or teachers’ salaries”, she told AFP.

In Strasbourg in the north-east, tram services were temporarily suspended to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”, the regional prefect said, after protesting students obstructed the tracks with crowd control barriers.

“There are 35 of us per classroom,” one 17-year-old Strasbourg student said. “There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms. The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources.”

Several bin fires were also reported in the southern city of Toulouse; while in Lille, young people wearing black hoodies destroyed a bus stop. In Marseille, there were attempts to light fires inside two schools. In one, a teacher was splashed with petrol.

While many teachers and several headteachers have reported being physically threatened and sometimes attacked, some support their pupils. Juliette Estiville, a high-school Spanish teacher in Paris, said that the police response had disgusted her.

“I’m actually here just to provide protection, to form a barrier between the police and the students,” she said. “Today went well, it’s going well, but I think that the teachers who come to the blockades are really there to protect our young people.”

The government has accused the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party of encouraging the protests, with several LFI MPs and mayors, including Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, cheered at demonstrations.

The party’s candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, insisted on Thursday that LFI backed “non-violent methods of struggle” and added that his “greatest worry is an unbearable level of police violence against these young people”.
output.standfirst: An internal investigation has opened into accusations that police used excessive force against three pupils, as nationwide school protests escalate into violence, with nearly 3,000 students detained and more than 300 police officers hurt.
output.progress: The interior ministry has opened an internal investigation into accusations of police brutality and excessive force against three pupils.

output.headline: No 10 insists no one is above the rules in Manchester City case
output.bodyHtml:
Downing Street has insisted that no one is above the rules in the Manchester City case, with a No 10 spokesperson saying on Thursday that the prime minister had made clear ‘the initial judgment is serious’ and that ‘there can’t be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules’.

The clarification came after Andy Burnham’s intervention in the Manchester City debate revived tension between the Premier League and the prime minister.

Government officials are understood to be unhappy they were not given notice that the independent commission’s judgment of £900m of financial manipulation and “sham contracts” would be published shortly after Burnham’s address to the Labour party conference on Tuesday, and his response has not gone down well with several Premier League clubs concerned by his relationship with City’s owners.

Related: Manchester City fans are right to feel angry – now they need to direct it at the owners | Will Unwin

In a series of interviews on Wednesday, Burnham said he would be ‘really concerned’ if City’s owners were forced to sell after being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of financial rules.

With City appealing against the verdict, the same No 10 spokesperson said the process had to be allowed to run its course, adding: ‘If wrongdoing is established those responsible should face the appropriate consequences.’ That phrase raised eyebrows, given City have already been found guilty by an independent commission after a 42-day hearing that produced 7,000 pages of witness evidence, eight years after the Premier League began investigating the club.

Burnham’s apparent sympathy for City, including a warning about jumping to conclusions and praise for the owners’ investment in Manchester, has alarmed some clubs, though the Premier League declined to respond.

HMRC is facing calls to get involved, with Meg Hillier, chair of the Treasury committee, asking for its response to the commission’s judgment. In a letter to John-Paul Marks, the permanent secretary of HMRC, Hillier sought assurances that the tax authority was ‘seized of the importance’ of the case and asked whether it had requested an unredacted copy of the commission’s verdict.

The Times and Daily Mail have reported that City’s appeal will be based on evidence the club claims proves its sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government and not the club. The commission rejected that argument as ‘untrue’.

Paragraph 77 of the judgment states: ‘We concluded that it was an “explanation” that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the Disguised Funding Scheme.’

Burnham has history with the Premier League, which he mentioned in Wednesday’s interviews by referencing his criticisms of its prosecution of his club, Everton, for financial rule breaches after they were docked 10 points – reduced to six on appeal – by an independent commission three years ago.

In November 2023, Burnham, when mayor of Greater Manchester, wrote to the Premier League chair, Alison Brittain, accusing the league of an ‘abuse of process’ and claimed Everton were being used as a pawn in efforts to show an independent regulator was not required in football.

Burnham made similar complaints on Wednesday despite Everton having admitted breaching profitability and sustainability rules, with the club contesting only the extent of the breach and sanction. ‘I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time and, with hindsight, I think more people would say that wasn’t fair the way that was handled,’ he said. ‘I still hold the view very firmly that they weren’t fairly treated in that process.’

The Premier League was unhappy with Burnham’s behaviour in 2023, particularly as his office posted on X two letters of complaint he had sent to the league, but did not publicise the replies sent by Brittain explaining the competition’s financial regulations governance process.

The Independent Football Regulator’s chief executive, David Kogan, has made clear he will not tolerate political interference in his role, telling the Times last year that he would resign if he sensed government pressure.

The City case has the potential to present an early test of his mettle and the IFR’s powers, given Burnham’s previous working relationship with the club’s owner, the Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), and the £25bn annual UK-Abu Dhabi trading relationship. One of Burnham’s first calls after he succeeded Sir Keir Starmer in July was with Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, president of the United Arab Emirates and the ultimate owner of ADUG.

Kogan confirmed the IFR was monitoring the case and has powers ‘to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives’ to protect ‘honesty and integrity of English football where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing by individuals’.

City’s owners are unlikely to fall foul of the licensing system that will be introduced next season, because that is an assessment of financial sustainability, separate from the new owners, directors and senior executives test, which the IFR uses to examine honesty and integrity.

The Premier League and IFR declined to comment.
captions: Football Weekly on Burnham, Guardiola and Manchester City
output.standfirst:
• Treasury committee chair wants HMRC involved in City case

  • Government said to be unhappy it was given no advance notice of the commission’s verdict on City’s £900m of financial manipulation
output.progress: Downing Street says nobody is above the rules, while the Treasury committee presses HMRC on the Manchester City case.

output.headline: Metropolitan police investigate Reform over foreign funding allegations
output.bodyHtml:
The Metropolitan police are carrying out a criminal investigation into Reform over allegations it broke foreign funding laws.

An undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News filmed some of Farage’s team appearing to plot to avoid electoral laws on foreign donations, rocking Reform on the eve of its party conference.

A group of investigative journalists called Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party.

In Channel 4 News’s investigation, footage showed that the fake UK-based supporter also had conversations with Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, who talked about commissioning polling that would be paid for by the US-based father.

In footage of another meeting, a senior adviser to Farage, Dan Jukes, appeared to suggest to the fake UK-based supporter that his US-based father could make a substantial donation by channelling it through the son.

Jukes has denied ‘any wrongdoing’ while Orr has said he would cooperate with the party’s internal investigation ‘fully’.

Meanwhile, Farage strongly hinted that Reform’s internal inquiry into the donations controversy that has overshadowed the party this year would absolve two key aides and that legal action would be launched against journalists involved.

Indicating that he had already seen the report and knew its conclusions, Farage said its release was ‘imminent’.

‘It’s been done. It’ll be out in public very soon and I think some of your co-conspirators might find themselves with one or two legal challenges,’ he told a Channel 4 journalist among reporters who questioned him.

Farage was speaking before a rally in the South Yorkshire city of Doncaster, the first of a series Reform is holding around Britain on the theme of what the party would do in its first 100 days of government.

Nigel Farage has claimed that Andy Burnham has given him ‘the biggest boost in my career’ by reviving the Brexit debate, which the Reform UK leader said had reopened a ‘huge flank’ to his party.

The prime minister’s pledges to the Labour conference and admission on Wednesday that rejoining the EU was among options the government would look at had put ‘put me back into the debate’, he said.

Looking tanned and relaxed before his party’s first major rally since its conference last month, Farage indicated to reporters that he was relishing a return to the playbook that he and others deployed during the 2016 referendum.

Polls show that as many as 59 per cent of the public favour rejoining the EU – a finding Farage dismissed, telling the Guardian: ‘Of course they do, until you tell them it’ll cost 25bn quid a year, until you tell him it’ll mean joining Schengen [the area of Europe that has open borders], until he tells them it will mean actually having to recommit to joining the euro.

‘Remember that the leavers haven’t made their arguments since 2016. The “remoaners” have made their arguments every single week. I mean, do you know what? I actually think that Burnham has made a very big political mistake here.’

While the Reform UK leader said he believed Burnham had calculated that new language on the EU might help win back voters from the Greens in big cities, Farage added: ‘Here in Doncaster and across the “red wall” in the north and Midlands, I think he’s opened up a huge flank to us.’

To cheers from hundreds of Reform supporters who gathered inside an event space at Doncaster racecourse, Farage said: ‘Today I’m back on the road and today is when our general election campaign starts.’

There were even bigger cheers when Farage said he would relish – ‘Bring it on, I say’ – the prospect of fighting Burnham in red wall areas such as Doncaster on the issue of rejoining the EU.

‘He might just have given me the biggest boost in my career I’ve ever had. Thank you, Andy, if you’re watching.’

The focus of the rally – ‘100 days to save Britain’ – had been planned before Burnham’s announcement about UK-EU relations. However, Reform sources claim that the prime minister’s intervention has energised them and that specific donors are already discussing how they can fund a rerun of the 2016 campaign.
output.standfirst:
Secretly filmed footage showed Reform aides discussing ways to channel money from a wealthy, impermissible American donor into the party, as the Metropolitan police separately investigate it over alleged breaches of foreign funding law.

  • UK politics live – latest updates
output.progress: Reform's internal investigation into the donations allegations is complete, with Farage saying its findings will be published imminently.

output.headline: Burnham moves to ban airlines from charging parents to sit with children
output.bodyHtml:
Parents will no longer be charged extra to sit with their children on planes, under new government plans to ban the practice.

The Department for Transport says sitting together can currently cost a parent and child up to £104 on a return journey.

The new rule would require airlines to seat passengers aged under 14 next to their parents or an accompanying adult free of charge, and passengers would no longer have to pay to correct a mistaken name on their flight booking.

Ministers are understood to be aiming to introduce the changes before the start of next year’s summer holidays. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said the rule changes are part of a crackdown on the “little charges that add up” when families plan their holidays.

MPs are debating a new set of rules for travel companies as the civil aviation (consumer protection and regulatory reform) bill makes its way through parliament, a law that would give ministers flexible power to set out passenger rights and the duties of airlines and airports.

Related: Burnham dodges questions on Heathrow third runway as project faces four-year delay

Burnham said: “Charging parents just to sit with their children is a rip-off, plain and simple. And being hit with a hefty fee for a simple spelling mistake on a booking form isn’t right either.

“People are fed up with these little charges that add up, so I’m putting a stop to them. This is what our everyday fixes are all about – giving people room to breathe by tackling the small irritations that catch people out, waste their time and cost them money.”

Rory Boland, editor of consumer magazine Which? Travel, said: “It’s clearly unfair to force parents and children as young as three to pay an extra fee just to sit together. Airlines that have separated families are putting profit ahead of passenger peace of mind.”

Ryanair had already adjusted its family seating policy earlier this year, after an investigation was launched into the company charging parents to sit with their children on flights. The Irish operator had previously required parents travelling with children aged between two and 11 to pay to reserve what was referred to as a mandatory family seat.

Children were then allocated seats next to or near their parents free of charge, after the UK Competition and Markets Authority watchdog found the fee for a mandatory family seat was typically about £8 each way.

Related: Ryanair will dispute passenger’s claim he was sucked out of window

Under the new policy, parents will still have the option of paying to reserve a seat of their choosing, with their children seated alongside them free of charge.

The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, has also announced a crackdown on bad behaviour by passengers on aircraft, with the government, airlines and trade unions working on a new system for sharing information about disruptive passengers.

Government figures show airlines logged more than 1,000 serious disruptive passenger incidents in 2025, including what it described as a mid-air brawl that caused a flight to be diverted.

Using the new system, airlines could choose to ban persistently disruptive passengers from their aircraft.
output.standfirst: Planned government rules will make airlines seat children under 14 beside parents for free, part of Burnham’s drive against ‘little charges that add up’ that can cost families up to £104 to sit together
output.progress: Ryanair adjusted its family-seating policy earlier this year, after a Competition and Markets Authority investigation into charging parents to sit with children.

output.headline: Flydubai passengers who saved stricken flight to receive heroism awards
output.bodyHtml:
Israeli passengers intervened to stop the attack on Wednesday, restraining the co-pilot, while a reserve crew in the plane stabilised the plummeting aircraft and landed it safely in Saudi Arabia.

Israeli officials praised the bravery of those who intervened and announced that four of the Israeli passengers would receive a 'heroism' award for preventing a potential disaster, on a plane that had more than 170 people onboard.

The Omani co-pilot who stabbed his captain in the apparent attempt to crash the Israel-bound flight from Dubai had previously undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was suicidal, Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has said.

Related: A ‘hero’ pilot, plumber and dentist among those who saved flydubai flight to Israel

Netanyahu told Fox News: 'We know that he underwent Islamic radical indoctrination. That appears to be something we are gathering from his personal information.'

Saudi security services were interrogating the co-pilot, whose identity is still not known, after arresting him on the plane's arrival in Tabuk, in the north-west of the country.

Saudi investigators were cooperating with the United Arab Emirates, the US, Oman and Israel to try to determine the attacker's motive, a regional official familiar with the investigation said. 'All possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into. Nothing is ruled out for now,' they told the Associated Press.

Two Israeli security officials said that Israel's initial assessment was that the co-pilot was probably acting alone, Reuters reported.

Netanyahu said that the co-pilot was probably suicidal, citing preliminary 'indications'.

'It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane … The Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that are found in his background, I think that's a pretty good clue,' he said, emphasising that final conclusions had yet to be made.

Two Israeli security sources told Reuters that they had not yet found any Iranian involvement in the attack; Netanyahu had previously said it was 'too early to say' if there was any state backing – namely Iranian.

The Israeli military had said before the incident it had no specific intelligence of an imminent threat, and the opposition leader Yair Lapid said a security briefing on Tuesday night included no mention of a related threat; the attack came just days after Netanyahu warned of an unspecified security threat to Israel that could come during its October election.

Other Israeli officials, including the defence minister, Israel Katz, and the ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, suggested the incident was a 'terror attack', with the Israeli foreign ministry briefing its diplomats that the attack was against Israel and its relationship with the UAE.

Donald Trump suggested the co-pilot was 'perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job', and told reporters at the White House that he and Netanyahu had spoken at length.

Netanyahu also spoke to the president of the UAE, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who agreed to Israel's involvement in the investigation.

Flydubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while the investigation took place and urged all parties 'to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts'.

The UAE announced on Thursday that it would conduct its own investigation into the incident, which started about two and a half hours after takeoff from Dubai. It said its investigators had begun to look into the attacker's motive and if he had any links to any 'terrorist purpose'.

The wounded pilot, Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, managed to send out an emergency signal and open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and stop the plane's descent, after passengers said they saw a knife-wielding man – apparently the Omani co-pilot – put the captain of the plane on the floor and the plane begin to plummet.

A video shared by the prime minister's office showed one passenger, Yaniv Hayoun, a plumber, speaking to Netanyahu at length about how the events onboard had played out.

Hayoun told the prime minister he and other passengers heard screaming and felt the air pressure change as the plane dived before they forced their way into the cockpit and found the attacker at the instrument panel. 'I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,' Hayoun said during the meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel.

Machchhar was widely praised for his bravery, with Netanyahu and the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, hailing him as a hero. India's ambassador to the UAE met the wounded captain's family and briefed them on his recovery, the Indian consulate in the UAE said.

Machchhar was being treated in a hospital in Tabuk, but was in good health and recovering well, according to the Indian embassy in the UAE, which said the ambassador had visited the pilot.

'Captain Smit Machchhar is a HERO,' Modi said, in a post on social media. 'In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others.'
output.standfirst: Israeli passengers and a reserve crew landed the plane safely after an Omani co-pilot allegedly stabbed the captain in an apparent attempt to crash it; he is now being interrogated by Saudi security services.
output.progress: Saudi, UAE, US, Omani and Israeli investigators are working together to establish the co-pilot's motive.

output.headline: Plan to help young people into work considered amid welfare overhaul
output.trail: Exclusive: A plan under discussion would give young people intensive support to help them into employment, as a key disability benefit for them faces being axed under wider welfare changes.
output.progress: A plan under discussion would give young disabled people intensive support to help them into employment.

output.headline: Counter-terrorism investigation leads to arrest over RAF Fairford incident
